# Interactive Volume Illustration (Hatching)

Also called: Hatching, Object space hatching, Stroke-based volume rendering, Two-Pass Hatching Rendering

## Overview
Interactive Volume Illustration (Hatching) is an object-space technique for illustrating volumetric data by simulating free-hand line art (hatching) using hardware-assisted [volume and line](#10926-dynamic-volume-lines-dvl.md) rendering [S2, unofficial]. It solves the problem of conveying shape and spatial relationships in 3D volumes by tracing hatches as polylines over implicit surfaces along either a fixed direction or a smoothed principal [curvature](#11695-curvature.md) direction [S1]. Unlike surface-based NPR methods where features are well-defined, this method determines feature areas through analysis of local volumetric properties because volumetric features vary continuously throughout three-dimensional space [G]. It sets itself apart from its siblings by explicitly combining line-strip primitives with [direct volume rendering](#1184-direct-volume-rendering.md) (DVR) in a two-pass pipeline, using data-driven seed point selection to minimize memory and generation time [S2, unofficial].

## How it works
The method operates in two main phases: stroke generation (preprocessing/seed placement) and rendering (two passes) [S2, unofficial].

### Inputs and Outputs
*   **Inputs:** 3D scalar volume data $V$, transfer function (for volume rendering), light direction $\vec{L}$, view direction $\vec{V}_{dir}$, user-defined fixed direction $\vec{s}_T$, smoothing weight $w_T$, flatness threshold $\epsilon$, cross-hatch angle threshold [S1][S2, unofficial].
*   **Outputs:** Final image combining hatching strokes and volumetric data [S2, unofficial].

### Data Structures
1.  **Volume Data:** 3D texture map or scalar grid [S2, unofficial].
2.  **Gradient/Normal Map:** Precomputed or on-the-fly gradients $\nabla f$ used to derive surface normals $\vec{N}$ and principal curvatures [S1][S2, unofficial].
3.  **Seed Points:** A set of 3D positions $\{p_j\}$ representing iso-surfaces, selected at run time to ensure an optimal number of points [S2, unofficial].
4.  **Stroke Buffer:** Stores line-strip primitives. Memory usage is at most one-eighth of the volume data set size [S2, unofficial].

### Step 1: Curvature Estimation and Smoothing
To guide hatches, principal curvature directions are computed [S1]. Direct tracing along raw principal curvature directions yields messy results when the main direction is not robustly defined [S1]. Therefore, the field is smoothed [S1].

1.  **Reconstruct Derivatives:** Use fast cubic B-spline filtering to reconstruct partial derivatives from volume data [S1].
2.  **Compute Principal Curvatures:** Calculate principal curvature magnitudes $\kappa_1, \kappa_2$ and shape index $s$ for each particle $p_j$ [S1].
    $$ s = \frac{2}{\pi} \arctan \left( \frac{\kappa_1 + \kappa_2}{\kappa_2 - \kappa_1} \right) $$
    where $\kappa_1 \ge \kappa_2$ and $|\kappa_1| + |\kappa_2| > 0$ [S1].
3.  **Compute Surface Reliability:** Determine if the local curvature is suitable for hatching [S1]:
    $$ \rho(\kappa_1, \kappa_2) = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } |\kappa_1| < \epsilon \text{ and } |\kappa_2| < \epsilon \\ 1 - |2(|s| - 1/2)| & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} $$
    Here $\epsilon$ defines which nearly flat surfaces are considered flat [S1].
4.  **Smooth Direction Field:** Compute the smoothed direction $\vec{s}_i$ for a particle $p_i$ by averaging the main principal curvature directions $\vec{\kappa}_{1j}$ of neighboring particles $p_j$ [S1]:
    $$ \vec{s}_i = w_T \frac{\sum_j \rho_j \vec{\kappa}_{1j}}{\sum_j \rho_j} + (1 - w_T) \vec{s}_T $$
    The trace reliability weight $w_T$ is determined by averaging the surface reliability of all neighboring particles:
    $$ w_T = \frac{\sum_j \rho_j}{\sum_j 1} $$
    This smoothing is executed on the GPU, estimating curvature information of neighboring particles on the fly [S1].

### Step 2: Stroke Generation (Object Space)
1.  **Seed Placement:** Select seed points at run time to represent iso-surfaces, ensuring an optimal number of points [S2, unofficial].
2.  **Trace Hatches:** In a [geometry shader](#4369-geometry-shader-quads.md), use particle positions as seed points. Determine vertices connecting hatch segments by projecting the smoothed direction $\vec{s}_i$ to the tangent plane [S1].
3.  **Store Strokes:** Represent hatches as line-strip primitives. These can be pre-computed since the approach is not view-dependent [S1].

### Step 3: Rendering (Two Passes)
**Pass 1: Render Hatching Strokes**
1.  Fetch line-strips from the texture buffer [S1].
2.  **Anisotropic Shading:** Illuminate using stored gradients. Apply anisotropic shading model for lines [S2, unofficial].
3.  **Front/Back Facing:** Determine orientation using surface normal $\vec{N}$ and view vector $\vec{V}$. Calculate two 2D lookup textures (varying diffuse/specular color). Interpolate color contributions based on $\vec{N} \cdot \vec{V}$ in the per-fragment shader [S2, unofficial].
4.  **Cross-Hatches:** For each seed, compute $\vec{N} \cdot \vec{L}$. If the angle is above a constant, generate an additional stroke along the minimal curvature direction. Cross-hatches are shorter than initial strokes [S2, unofficial].
5.  **Depth Test:** Enable depth test and update depth buffer. Render transparent volume structures in back-to-front order without changing OpenGL state [S2, unofficial].

**Pass 2: Render Volumetric Data**
1.  Render the volumetric data set using 3D texture maps (Direct Volume Rendering) [S2, unofficial].
2.  **Alpha/Depth Test:** Use alpha-test and depth-test during re-sampling to render only texture samples closest to the viewpoint and above/below a threshold [S2, unofficial].
3.  **Hatch Visibility:** To ensure only hatches in front of the iso-surface remain visible for opaque rendering, write white color to the frame buffer after rendering hatches, then render [volume with alpha](#2510-sample-opacities-from-mask.md)/depth test [S2, unofficial].

### Pseudocode
> **Unverified code.** The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors.

```python
import math

def compute_shape_index(k1, k2):
    if abs(k1) + abs(k2) == 0:
        return 0.0
    return (2.0 / math.pi) * math.atan((k1 + k2) / (k2 - k1))

def compute_surface_reliability(k1, k2, s, epsilon):
    if abs(k1) < epsilon and abs(k2) < epsilon:
        return 0.0
    return 1.0 - abs(2.0 * (abs(s) - 0.5))

def project_to_tangent_plane(direction, normal):
    dot = sum(d * n for d, n in zip(direction, normal))
    return [direction[i] - dot * normal[i] for i in range(3)]

def find_nearest_particle(position, particles):

def interpolate_lookup_texture(dot_nv):

def draw_line(p1, p2, color):

def enable_depth_test():

def depth_test_pass(position):

def write_white_to_framebuffer():
    # Writes white color to frame buffer [S2, unofficial]
    pass

def generate_hatching_strokes(seeds, normals, s_T, epsilon, max_segments=10):
    line_strips = []
    for i, seed in enumerate(seeds):
        normal = normals[i]
        smoothed_dir = [1.0, 0.0, 0.0] # Computed from neighbors [G]
        dir_on_plane = project_to_tangent_plane(smoothed_dir, normal)
        
        strip = [seed]
        current_pos = seed
        current_dir = dir_on_plane
        for _ in range(max_segments):
            next_pos = [current_pos[j] + current_dir[j] for j in range(3)]
            strip.append(next_pos)
            current_pos = next_pos
            new_normal = normals[find_nearest_particle(current_pos, seeds)]
            new_smoothed = [1.0, 0.0, 0.0] # Computed from neighbors [G]
            current_dir = project_to_tangent_plane(new_smoothed, new_normal)
        line_strips.append(strip)
    return line_strips

def render_strokes(line_strips, normals, view_vector, light_direction, cross_hatch_threshold, seeds):
    for strip in line_strips:
        for i in range(len(strip) - 1):
            p1, p2 = strip[i], strip[i+1]
            normal = normals[find_nearest_particle(p1, seeds)]
            
            dot_nv = sum(n * v for n, v in zip(normal, view_vector))
            color = interpolate_lookup_texture(dot_nv)
            
            if dot_nv > 0:
                color = [0.0, 0.0, 1.0] # Front facing blue [S2, unofficial]
            else:
                color = [1.0, 1.0, 0.0] # Back facing yellow [S2, unofficial]
                
            draw_line(p1, p2, color)
            
            dot_nl = sum(n * l for n, l in zip(normal, light_direction))
            angle = math.acos(max(-1.0, min(1.0, dot_nl)))
            if angle > cross_hatch_threshold:
                cross_dir = [0.0, 1.0, 0.0] # Minimal curvature direction [G]
                cross_strip = generate_hatching_strokes([p1], [normal], cross_dir, 0.0, max_segments=5) # Shorter [S2, unofficial]
                render_strokes(cross_strip, normals, view_vector, light_direction, cross_hatch_threshold, seeds)
                
    enable_depth_test()

def render_volume(volume_data, threshold):
    for sample in volume_data.back_to_front():
        if sample.value > threshold:
            alpha = sample.alpha
            if depth_test_pass(sample.position):
                draw_sample(sample, alpha)
    write_white_to_framebuffer()
```

### Parameters and Typical Values
*   **$\epsilon$:** Parameter defining which nearly flat surfaces are considered flat. Not given in the sources.
*   **$w_T$:** Smoothing weight. Not given in the sources.
*   **Viewport Resolution:** 600x600 pixels [S2, unofficial].
*   **Strokes per Example:** 20K to 50K strokes generated [S2, unofficial].
*   **Average Line Segments:** 10 line segments per stroke [S2, unofficial].
*   **Memory Usage:** At most one eighth of the memory consumed by the volume data set is required to store the selected strokes [S2, unofficial].

### Edge Cases and Pitfalls
*   **Messy Results:** Directly tracing along principal curvature directions yields messy results when the main direction is not robustly defined [S1]. Smoothing is required.
*   **Hatch Visibility:** To ensure only hatches in front of the iso-surface remain visible for opaque rendering, write white color into the frame buffer after rendering hatches, then render volume with alpha/depth test [S2, unofficial].
*   **Intersections:** Long hatch strokes might lead to intersections [S1].

## Subtopics

### Object-space hatching lines
A non-photorealistic technique combining line drawings with direct volume rendering (DVR) by placing hatching lines along principal curvature directions of structures before [compositing](#2436-compositing.md) with the volume model [S3, unofficial]. It involves identifying structures of interest, computing principal curvature directions, generating hatching lines aligned with these directions in object space, and combining them with the direct volume rendering of the volume model [S3, unofficial].

## Operating characteristics
*   **Time Complexity:** Preprocessing time is significant for large datasets (1.3 minutes for a $256^3$ volume dataset, including curvature estimation and octree construction) [S2, unofficial]. Seed placement takes between 0.5 and 4 seconds [S2, unofficial].
*   **Memory Complexity:** Memory usage is at most one-eighth of the volume data set size to store selected strokes [S2, unofficial].
*   **Performance:** Rendering performance is 4 to 8 fps for various datasets (engine block, hydrogen molecule, iron protein, aneurysm, human foot, human skull) on a 600x600 viewport [S2, unofficial]. Toon shader performance is about 7 fps [S2, unofficial].
*   **Strengths:** Interactive, hardware-assisted, minimizes memory and generation time via data-driven seed point selection, effectively conveys shape and spatial correlations [S2, unofficial].
*   **Limitations:** Direct curvature tracing can be messy without smoothing [S1].

## Background
The method was presented by R.F.P. van Pelt, A. Vilanova, and H.M.M. van de Wetering in 2008 [S1]. It builds on the work of Sigg and Hadwiger [SH05] for fast cubic B-spline filtering [S1] and anisotropic [shading models](#837-shading-models.md) for lines [S2, unofficial]. The shape index was introduced by Koenderink and Van Doorn [KvD92] [S1]. The technique is part of the broader field of interactive non-photorealistic volume rendering, aiming to bring NPR techniques and real-time 3D graphics to the visualization community [S2, unofficial].
